series: LINUX PERMISSIONS: A FIELD HANDBOOK — PART 2

blocks.title: Sticky Guards The Entry Only
blocks.text: Without it, any user could delete or replace your /tmp files. With it, a writable file's CONTENTS can still be overwritten in place.

items: Symlink and hardlink races are what is left.
fs.protected_symlinks and _hardlinks mitigate, on by default.
Use mkstemp(3) or mktemp, never a predictable name.
"alice and bob write, carol reads" needs a new group.
ACLs add per-user and per-group entries instead.
Needs fs support and the acl mount option.
Default on modern ext4, xfs, btrfs.
A + after the mode in ls -l means an ACL exists.
user::, user:name:, group::, group:name:
mask::, other::
Named entries are the whole point of ACLs.

blocks.title: The Mask Is A Ceiling
blocks.text: Every named user, named group, and group:: entry is ANDed with mask::. getfacl prints #effective: on any entry the mask clips.

blocks.title: The Biggest ACL Trap
items: chmod's group digit rewrites the MASK, not group::.
So chmod 750 can silently disable live ACL entries.
Always run getfacl after chmod on an ACL file.

lines: # then repeat with -d for future files

items: Defaults change nothing about the directory's own access.
Every new child inherits the entry instead.
Inherited entries override umask for new files.
Check order: owner, named users, groups (masked), other.
Named-user entries beat any group entry.
cp drops ACLs unless -a or --preserve=all.
tar needs --acls; rsync needs -A.
Backups losing ACLs silently is very common.

blocks.title: Groups Coarse, ACLs Narrow
blocks.text: ACLs are precise but invisible past one + in ls -l, and they drift. Use groups for policy, ACLs for exceptions.

items: Path resolution demands MAY_EXEC on every component.
Then generic_permission() on the target inode.
fsuid == owner: use user bits and stop.
Else GID in the credential set: group bits and stop.
Else other bits. First match, never best match.

lines: # binds port 80 with no root at all

items: LSM hooks run after DAC: SELinux or AppArmor may deny.
Denied with correct-looking modes = LSM, nosuid or ro.
Mount options ro, noexec, nosuid, nodev always win.
vfat/ntfs fake modes via uid=, gid=, umask=, fmask=, dmask=.
chmod on those filesystems fails or does nothing.
NFS root_squash maps remote root to nobody.
Client attribute caching delays visible mode changes.

lines: id; stat f; mount | grep /srv; getfacl f

items: chmod -R 777 "to make it work": model defeated.
On a web root, any local process rewrites your code.
chmod -R 644 . strips dir x and bricks the tree.
Use -R a+rX for the recursive read case.
Expecting fall-through: chmod 077 locks the owner out.
640 owned by the service still fails for the service —
owner class matched first, group bits never read.
Correct file mode, no x on a parent: traversal forgotten.
setuid on a shell script: silently ignored. Use sudoers.
New umask, old files: umask is creation-time only.
chmod on an ACL file wrecks the mask — verify with getfacl.
Writable dir + read-only file: delete and replace wins.
Protect the directory, not only the file.
scp drops setuid and can widen modes.
rsync -a keeps standard bits; add -A -X for ACLs, xattrs.
Container UID 999 cannot write a host dir owned by 1000.

blocks.title: Editors Rewrite Files
blocks.text: Write-temp-then-rename creates a NEW inode with your umask. The original mode, owner and ACLs are gone.

items: 644 / 755 baseline, 640 / 750 for service data.
600 / 700 for secrets, 400 for read-only keys.
Treat 777, world-writable dirs and stray setuid as findings.
u+x add owner execute; go-w drop group/other write.
a=r everyone read-only; +t sticky.
u+s setuid; g+s setgid.
Inspect with ls -l, stat, namei -l, getfacl, id, lsattr.
Web: files 644, dirs 755, owned by the deploy user.
Group-readable by the web server user only.
The web server must never own the code it serves.
SSH: ~/.ssh 700, keys 600, authorized_keys 600.
Home must not be group- or world-writable, or sshd refuses.

blocks.title: Three Questions Solve Almost Everything
blocks.text: Who is the process (id)? What does the path require at every component (namei -l)? Is something above the filesystem overriding it — mount options, SELinux, container UID mapping?

caption.text: Part 2 of LINUX PERMISSIONS: A FIELD HANDBOOK. chmod -R 777 is not a fix, it is a confession. This handbook walks the whole Linux permission model end to end — the nine bits, why x on a directory means search and not execute, octal by hand, umask as a bit-clear rather than a subtraction, setuid, the sticky bit, POSIX ACLs and their mask trap, and the exact order the kernel checks. Ten pages of dense field notes, including the three questions that diagnose nearly every permission bug.
